newsitem.title: INDIA: India stocks await bank policy, fear 1st half results.
newsitem.headline: India stocks await bank policy, fear 1st half results.

text.p: India's upcoming monetary policy announcement is expected to drive down interest rates and cheer stock markets, but a sharp rally is unlikely as first half company results begin to roll in, analysts said on Tuesday.

They said the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is likely to ease liquidity by announcing a one percent cut in the cash reserve requirements of banks when it releases its credit policy for the second half of 1996/97 (April-March) on Saturday.
"We expect an easing in interest rates," said K.R. Bharat, deputy managing director at Peregrine Capital India.
"India has one of the highest real interest rates in the world and with the current deceleration we expect the RBI will do everything to stimulate economic activity," he said.
Interest rates for top-rated borrowers range from 15.5 to 19.0 percent per annum. Inflation as measured by the wholesale price index was at 6.34 percent in September.

Analysts say tight money conditions in late 1995 combined with political uncertainty in the run-up to general elections earlier this year resulted in an industrial slowing in the first half of 1996/97 (April-March).

Ritu Gupte, strategist at Jardine Fleming India Broking, said the economic deceleration was a result of a slowdown in demand for funds due to the high interest rate scenario, infrastructure bottlenecks and political uncertainty.
"The main aim is to bring interest rates down. The RBI has to decide whether they want growth or inflation," Gupte said.

Plunging global prices of key commodities and the imposition of a 12.9 percent minimum tax on previously untaxed company profits have added to the woes with a sharp slowdown expected in the first-half profits of leading Indian firms.
Among the worst hit is Reliance Industries which is expected to announce a sharp fall in net profits for the six months ended September 30, 1996.
"In the short-term, Reliance could be more important for the market than any cut in cash reserve ratios," one analyst said.
Results from the petrochemicals giant are due on Friday.

"We believe that corporate slowdown has not adequately been factored into share prices and there is still considerable downside, give the rather fragile state of the economy," a leading investment bank said in its latest monthly report.

"The market has sensed (but not sufficiently discounted) the tremors that will arise out of political chaos, an impending economic recession and disappearing corporate growth in coming months. This will lead to a turbulent October in the stockmarket, leading to further disenchantment for investors," the report said.
